title: What did the fire do to the air?
subtitle: Saffire IV–VI cabin atmosphere, heat release, and smoke detection evidence in unmanned Cygnus spacecraft
boundary_statements: This case study presents traceable published results from unmanned Cygnus Saffire IV–VI experiments and related SAME/Fortenberry detection research; it is not a fire-safety certification, material ranking, or human crew exposure calculation.
Strictly isolated from PSI-99 (SAFFIRE-II 9 physical sample cards), PSI-39 (CFI), FLEX droplet prediction, and the 403 core PSI-25/PSI-69 dataset.

Table 2 gas values represent campaign/event concentration or partial-pressure increases measured near the Far Field Diagnostics (FFD) inlet, not baseline-plus-fire crew exposure levels inside an inhabited habitat.
Blank or missing cells for V-3 and V-4 gas/calorimetry fields are preserved as null/unreported and never coerced to zero.

Ambient oxygen partial pressure (pO2_kPa = pressure_kPa * oxygen_mol_percent / 100) and the VI-3 elapsed delta between ignition (637 s) and 1 mg/m3 threshold crossing (981 s -> 344 s) are explicitly tagged as derived values rather than verbatim NASA metrics.
what_this_does_not_establish: Does not certify crew survival limits, habitability safety compliance, or safe exposure durations with or without cabin scrubbing.
Does not provide a full gas or heat-release dataset for Saffire V-3 or V-4 (neither appears in NTRS 20240002981 Table 1/2 gas or calorimetry results).
Does not establish quantitative false-alarm or detection percentages from the paywalled Fire Safety Journal article (DOI: 10.1016/j.firesaf.2018.04.004 full text was not accessed).
Does not extrapolate microgravity Cygnus results (16.7–19.0 m3 unmanned spacecraft) directly to partial-gravity Lunar (1/6g) or Martian (3/8g) habitats without physical validation.

detection_evidence.title: Saffire VI-3 authors' selected smoke-concentration threshold (981 s at 1 mg/m³)
detection_evidence.derived_note: Derived elapsed time 344 s (= 981 s - 637 s) from slide-annotated ignition (20240007488 slides 16–18) and NTRS-reported authors' selected 1 mg/m³ tight alarm threshold crossing (20240002981 p.5). It is not verbatim labeled 'alarm latency' by NASA.
detection_evidence.summary: In Saffire VI-3, the authors report crossing their selected 1 mg/m³ smoke-concentration criterion at 981 s, after much hazardous gas release. Figure 7 separately plots ionization-detector voltage and DustTrak mass concentration.
detection_evidence.limitations: The selected mass-concentration criterion is not a demonstrated calibrated ionization-detector alarm setting. These FFD measurements in unmanned Cygnus do not establish crewed ISS/Orion operational alarm logic.

detection_evidence.title: SAME / SAME-2 (ISS): No single detector fits all smoke particle sizes
detection_evidence.summary: Overheated cellulose, Kapton, silicone rubber, Teflon, and Pyrell in ISS microgravity showed strong detector bias by particle size: the ISS light-scattering photoelectric detector easily picked up larger particles from cellulose, silicone, and Pyrell but frequently failed to detect smaller particles from Teflon and Kapton (widely used in electronics); the Shuttle ionization detector fared slightly better for Teflon and submicron particulate.
detection_evidence.limitations: Primary verification comes from public NIST release (May 1, 2018), local AIAA 2012-3536 SAME-2 paper (20130000422), and Fortenberry NTRS 20220009167 slide 7. Fire Safety Journal Vol. 98 pp.74–81 full text (DOI 10.1016/j.firesaf.2018.04.004) is paywalled and unread; quantitative percentage sensitivity figures are omitted.

detection_evidence.summary: Particle mass concentration at the Far Field Diagnostics unit was dominated by submicron particles (PM1, dp <= 1 µm) across all five measured burn events in Saffire IV and V, while PMMA burns produced higher concentrations of larger particles (dp > 4 µm) compared with SIBAL or cotton jersey.
detection_evidence.limitations: Crucial experimental caveat on slide 13: avionics temperatures and imagery indicated clogging of the SFU outlet screen, meaning FFD measurements likely missed a significant fraction of larger particles.

passages.section_title: Saffire VI Experimental Hardware & IV/V Calorimetry Limitation
passages.source_text: Saffire IV–VI spanned 1.5 to 3.2 kW fires across 17 to 19 m³ free air volumes in orbiting Cygnus vehicles (samples 41 cm wide; SIBAL cloth 50 cm long; 2-sided PMMA 1 cm thick, 18 cm long; 1-sided PMMA 0.5 cm thick, 18 cm long). On Saffire IV and V, the SFU outlet gas sensor had been moved from the verified mixing location so outlet gas measurements could not provide oxygen-consumption calorimetry for high-heat-release PMMA tests; for Saffire VI the sensor was moved back to the verified mixed outlet location.

passages.section_title: Table 1 Test Conditions (IV-1, V-2, VI-2, VI-3, VI-4)
passages.source_text: Before testing, Cygnus free volume was measured by CO2 release, followed by venting and O2 backfill. Executed conditions in Table 1: IV-1 (SIBAL, 50 cm, 20 cm/s Concurrent, 100.0 kPa, 22.0 mol% O2, 17.9 m³); V-2 (Cotton Jersey, 50 cm, 20 cm/s Concurrent, 70.7 kPa, 26.2 mol% O2, 19.0 m³); VI-2 (SIBAL, 50 cm, 20 cm/s Concurrent, 54.1 kPa, 31.0 mol% O2, 16.7 m³); VI-3 (Two-Sided PMMA, 18 cm, 20 cm/s Concurrent, 54.6 kPa, 30.3 mol% O2, 16.7 m³); VI-4 (One-Sided PMMA, 18 cm, 20 cm/s Concurrent, 55.2 kPa, 28.8 mol% O2, 16.7 m³). Nomex on Saffire VI did not ignite.

passages.section_title: Heat Release Dual Methods (Oxygen vs Fuel Consumption Calorimetry)
passages.source_text: Heat release was calculated from oxygen consumption using Huggett's factor of 13.1 kJ per gram of oxygen consumed (Table 2: VI-2 peak 3217 W / 580 kJ total; VI-3 peak 3080 W / 1280 kJ total; VI-4 peak 1507 W / 830 kJ total). Fuel consumption calorimetry estimated heat release from fuel consumption / spread rate for thin materials (IV-1 avg 3150 W / 409 kJ; V-2 avg 2800 W / 560 kJ; VI-2 avg 3650 W / 409 kJ). For thick PMMA slabs, surface regression obscures burning rate from cameras so fuel-consumption calorimetry is omitted. For VI-2 SIBAL both methods were used and authors state they agree within 15%.

passages.section_title: Saffire VI-3 Flow Schedule, 981 s Detection Threshold, and SMAC / NASA-STD-3001 Comparison
passages.source_text: Curated paraphrase, not a verbatim quotation. In Saffire VI-3 (two-sided PMMA), duct flow was reduced from 20 cm/s to 5 cm/s at 1120 s and terminated at 1420 s; under 5 cm/s flow, SFU outlet CO2 and CO rose higher. The authors report crossing their selected smoke mass concentration criterion of 1 mg/m³ at 981 s, after much hazardous gas release. Figure 7 separately plots ionization-detector voltage and DustTrak mass concentration; this does not establish a calibrated ionization-alarm setting in mg/m³. Near the FFD, temperature rose only slightly (20–25 °C vs 45–77 °C at SFU outlet). The authors compare CO increases with CO SMAC benchmarks (24-hour: 100 ppm; 1-hour: 425 ppm, JSC 20584 Rev A) and CO2 increases with the 3 mmHg 1-hour average limit in NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev D. Table 2 reports ΔCO = 80, 83, 120, 308, 320 ppm and ΔCO2 = 3.51 mmHg for VI-3 and 3.37 mmHg for VI-4. These reported increases do not establish time-averaged human exposure or a crew exposure-limit violation. Thin fuels had lower ΔCO2 (1390–2800 ppm, 1.03–1.26 mmHg) and ΔCO (80–120 ppm) than thick PMMA (8117–8539 ppm CO2, 3.37–3.51 mmHg, 308–320 ppm CO).

passages.section_title: Saffire VI-3 Ignition at 637 s, Flow Steps, and Conclusions
passages.source_text: Saffire VI flew in December 2023 (Saffire IV in May 2020, Saffire V in January 2021). Slides 16–18 annotate Saffire VI-3 traces: Ignition at 637 s, flow reduced from 20 cm/s to 5 cm/s at 1120 s, and duct flow terminated at 1420 s. Slide 20 lists Table 2 alongside the 3 mmHg 1-hour CO2 limit and 425 ppm (1-hour) / 100 ppm (24-hour) CO limits. Slide 21 concludes heat from these 1.5–3.2 kW spacecraft fires was localized near the fire, while smoke and gaseous products were the principal hazard.

passages.section_title: Saffire V-3 and V-4 Conditions and Unreported Gas/Heat Status
passages.source_text: NTRS 20210011521 (ICES-2021-266) Table 1 (p.3) documents V-3 (1-sided 5 mm PMMA, 18 cm long, 20 cm/s concurrent flow, 71.3 kPa, 25.4 mol% O2, 19.0 m³ free volume) and V-4 (structured ribbed PMMA 1–10 mm ribs / 3 mm high, 20 cm long, 20 cm/s opposed flow, 72.6 kPa, 25.7 mol% O2, 19.0 m³ free volume). On p.5–6, reducing flow from 20 cm/s to 5 cm/s for 300 s cooled V-3 and V-4 enough for immediate extinction when fan stopped. On p.7 Fig.8, V-4 exhibited an initial ignition deflagration (~645 s radiometer peak, expanding in 100 ms). On p.9, V-3 concurrent PMMA flame grew to a limiting 11 cm length after 450 s. Neither V-3 nor V-4 has published gas (CO/CO2) or calorimetry values in NTRS 20240002981.

passages.section_title: SAME ISS Detector Size Bias (Meyer / Cleary, NIST May 1, 2018)
passages.source_text: In the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) on the ISS (2007 and 2010), overheated cellulose, Kapton, silicone rubber, Teflon, and Pyrell were tested across heating rates, flows (up to 8 cm/s vs zero flow), and aging. Lead author Marit Meyer reported that the ISS light-scattering photoelectric detector easily detected larger particles from cellulose, silicone, and Pyrell, but frequently failed to detect smaller smoke particles from Teflon and Kapton (used heavily in electronics), while the Space Shuttle ionization detector fared only slightly better for Teflon. Researchers concluded no single current detection method detects all smoke particle sizes.

passages.section_title: Fortenberry (2022): Saffire IV–V Submicron PM1 Dominance & Screen Clogging
passages.source_text: Claire Fortenberry (USRA / NASA GRC, June 15, 2022) slides 11–14 show DustTrak DRX (PM1, PM2.5, PM4, PM10) and modified First Alert ionization chamber measurements at FFD in Saffire IV and V. Particle mass concentration was dominated by submicron particles (PM1, dp <= 1 µm) across all five burn events measured. PMMA events produced higher concentrations of larger particles (dp > 4 µm) compared to SIBAL or cotton jersey. However, slide 13 explicitly warns that avionics temperatures and imagery indicated clogging of the SFU outlet screen, so FFD measurements likely missed a significant fraction of larger particles.

passages.section_title: SAME-2 Expedition 24 Aerosol Moments and Ionization vs Light Scattering Sensitivity
passages.source_text: SAME-2 (Expedition 24, July–September 2010) measured zero-, first-, and third-moment smoke aerosol distributions from Teflon, Kapton, cotton lampwick, silicone rubber, and Pyrell across 0–8 cm/s flow and 11–1800 s aging. Average smoke particle sizes were mostly 200–400 nm (larger by 2–3x for zero flow vs 8 cm/s flow). Space Shuttle ionization detectors (proportional to first moment) readily detected submicron particulates from all five materials, whereas ISS near-IR forward scattering detectors are most sensitive to particles larger than 1 µm.
